title: Reimagining Litigation Workflows through AI: A Panel Recorded Live at the Everlaw Summit
author: Everlaw Summit panelists

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source documents uneven AI adoption, tool selection, affordability and general concerns about output trust and job security. It does not substantively address whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship, creates a verification-experience paradox, or requires reconstructed training through simulation, mentorship and independent practice.
qs: Whether attorneys can really trust the outputs from these systems and [music] what this technology means for the future of legal work and job security.
Uh and that's that's probably lawyers and lit support people alike as they look at this technology.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source provides anecdotal evidence about uneven AI experimentation, selective tool procurement and scale-sensitive costs in commercial litigation. Those observations align with peripheral cluster distinctions between adoption, deployment and affordability, but the source does not address whether AI can expand meaningful legal help or whether uptake can close the justice gap.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the process-led redesign proposition and materially extends it with a concrete firm-wide implementation model: dedicated staff map every practice group’s processes, then apply generative AI or other automation selectively within streamlined workflows. It also reinforces the cluster’s view that organisational capability and tool evaluation—not mere model access—are the immediate bottlenecks, while offering no measured productivity or employment outcomes.
qs: We have a team of about 10 people in our information management team that are doing the process mapping for every single practice group.

And what's going to come out of that is not just where can we put Gen AI, but where can we use automation, where can we um so we'll be creating these streamlined workflows and then applying the technology where we need it.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that practical AI value depends on institutional commitment and selective implementation rather than mere tool access. It materially extends the cluster by adding procurement evidence—broad platform evaluation—and a cost-scaling distinction between affordable individual tasks and expensive document-scale deployment, while offering little evidence on verification, workflow redesign or labour effects.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s organizational-change framing and materially develops it with a concrete implementation method: map routine legal work and handoffs before identifying where AI fits. Its experience with a deposition application developed in isolation also illustrates why promising tools must be connected to earlier case information and end-to-end workflows. It reports implementation experience rather than measured efficiency gains.

So, we're I'm currently working with Julie and we're in the process and and others, but we're in the process of writing down just what we do in brief snippets, you know, from associate to partner to client to court to opposing council where the work goes and we're now starting to in the last month or so identify the areas that AI will fit in.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s conditional optimism: it presents AI as personally energising and recommends thoughtful engagement, while offering anecdotal experience rather than demonstrated customer outcomes, adoption methods or broader workforce evidence.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of bounded agent experimentation combined with workflow redesign and uneven organisational readiness. st.an: The source supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition by describing agent building alongside firm-wide process mapping and selective use of AI or other automation. It also notes uneven adoption and questions transferability to less technologically prepared firms, but these are qualifications rather than opposition.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of generative AI addressing a specific legal workflow and of adoption depending on organisational circumstances and operational need. Its reported success is anecdotal and undefined, so it does not substantiate the stronger claims about durable specialist workflow-layer value, lawyer–engineer collaboration or verified copilot design.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The panel directly supports the cluster’s workflow-first, lawyer-guided framing: it advocates mapping existing litigation workflows before adopting AI and conditions faster discovery insights on human accuracy verification and legally defensible provenance and decision records. Its evidence is qualitative practitioner experience rather than measured comparative performance.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of selective, task-specific augmentation and uneven organisational adoption through an anecdote about using generative AI for coding suggestions when conventional review was impracticable. Its support is limited: it reports initial success without metrics, verification procedures, or evidence about junior development and staffing leverage.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The panel supports the cluster’s emphasis on bounded, task-level automation and uneven institutional adoption. Its litigation examples show AI being used selectively where conventional review was infeasible, while extensive tool evaluation, trust concerns and scale-dependent costs reinforce the case for controlled implementation rather than autonomous legal delivery.
qs: Manual review would be no way would be possible.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The panel aligns closely with the synthesis: it reports gains in bounded litigation and document-review tasks while treating adoption as experimental, requiring workflow integration, training, secure handling, verification and defensibility. It also preserves lawyers’ responsibility for judgment, strategy and client-facing work rather than predicting wholesale replacement.
qs: And so as we move forward, let's say about six months, those same kinds of organizations, we're now beginning to think, oh, how can I integrate this into my overall first pass review, how do I think about that process to be able to do that and do this systematically, not just in the situations where my back is against the wall, where I can really apply this much more broadly.
So understanding what it's  capable of, verifying its accuracy is kind of where we are.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The panel supports treating trust as a workflow property: AI can be adopted for bounded document tasks while lawyers validate outputs and build confidence through testing on familiar matters. It also rejects error-free reliability claims by acknowledging persistent hallucination risk; its evidence is experiential rather than quantified.
qs: >> We admit and I think any provider who  says we can eliminate hallucinations 100% is not telling the truth.

kp.k: Map existing workflows before choosing AI interventions
kp.d: Adam describes sidestepping adoption pressure by documenting work from associate through partner, client, court and opposing counsel before identifying AI opportunities. Julie reports a parallel approach: responding immediately to specific problems by building agents while an information management team of about 10 people maps every practice group's processes. The aim includes conventional automation, not just generative AI.
qs: we kind of sidestepped the urgency because we realized that the bigger question we needed to be asking is what are we currently doing?
We have a team of about 10 people in our information management team that are doing the process mapping for every single practice group.
what's going to come out of that is not just where can we put Gen AI, but where can we use automation

kp.k: Adoption requires policies, training and institutional support
kp.d: Julie recalls quickly creating a policy on public tools after ChatGPT's November 2022 debut, an attorney workshop in July or August 2023, and purchases of tools considered safe in January 2024; she qualifies these dates with recollections. A technology adoption group develops training. Joshua reports substantial variation among customers, including organizations without policies and greater potential complications in the public sector; these are market observations, not survey findings.
qs: in November of um 2022 I believe when chat GPT made its debut we were pretty quick to create a policy first of all about using publicly available tools.
We have a technology adoption group. So they've been involved in developing training programs.
on the public sector side I think that can get even more complicated.

kp.k: Early insight gains precede broader time savings
kp.d: Julie reports that AI is surfacing insights attorneys might otherwise miss, while training, prompting and iteration still consume time. She distinguishes already observed document-review cost or time savings from broader drafting and task efficiencies, which she expects within six months rather than claims to have demonstrated. No quantified productivity study is supplied.
qs: it's providing our attorneys with insights that they may not have seen.
I figure probably within six months we'll start to see more time savings.
Obviously on document review we've already seen some of the the cost savings or time savings there.

kp.k: Deposition experiment illustrates connections requiring lawyer judgment
kp.d: Adam describes testing deposition-summary functionality on a resolved case he knew thoroughly. The tool flagged a connection between testimony about medication and taking Tums. He treats this as a promising language-based proof of concept, not a useful impeachment point: AI supplies possible follow-up items while the attorney selects legally meaningful strategy. The panel explicitly clarifies that this was deposition summary, not Deep Dive.
qs: We we set up a sandbox environment with the files that on a case that I had recently resolved and I knew everything inside and out.
I'm not going to go impeach them with that at trial.
I had a register of things that I could then go through and and do that bespoke legal strategy, make those decisions.

kp.k: Deep Dive offers corpus-scale questioning with source links
kp.d: Joshua describes the newly generally released Deep Dive as natural-language questioning across a document corpus, with the largest beta matter containing 10 million documents. Answers link to cited documents and include tables distinguishing degrees of relevance to support human verification. Julie reports that her firm's first test used 300,000 documents and impressed the team; these are vendor capability claims and practitioner experience, not measured accuracy or completeness results.
qs: deep dive allows you to ask natural language questions of a full document corpus.
the largest matter that we had in the beta was 10 million documents.
you can link back directly to the documents that it's citing.
our our first test case was 300,000 documents

kp.k: Investigation, review checks and deposition preparation are current uses
kp.d: Julie identifies actual uses of Deep Dive: finding people and events in investigations, explaining document selection, checking for material missed by search strings or predictive coding, and preparing depositions by investigating knowledge and conflicting documents. The reported quality-control use supplements existing review methods; the transcript does not establish measured recall improvements.
qs: when you're doing an investigation, you're just trying to figure out who are the people, who are the events, what's going on, what happened.
after we've done um predictive coding, we've went back in and said, "What did we miss? Did we miss anything?"
Are there documents that conflict what they think they know about it? Those kind of questions can all be asked with deep dive.

kp.k: Strategic advantage remains conditional and partly prospective
kp.d: Adam anticipates using corpus questioning to identify opponents' strongest arguments and evidence harmful to the defense, potentially shifting differentiation toward strategy and presentation once both sides possess similar tools. He expressly says this strategic scenario is not yet playing out. His claimed competitive advantage is conditional on verifying accuracy and being able to explain discovery decisions, authenticity and chain of custody defensibly.
qs: the more important information is what's harmful for the defense.
theoretically I it's not playing out yet
what decisions we made regarding discovery are something we can write about in a declaration in motion practice.
But yes, if you can prove it up and it's right

kp.k: Emergency experiments can become systematic first-pass review
kp.d: Joshua reports that approximately six months earlier customers initially tried generative coding suggestions when deadlines made ordinary review infeasible. He says successful experiments prompted consideration of routine first-pass integration. He also relays a customer's example of rapidly processing a last-minute production before a deposition; this is vendor-carried customer testimony rather than independently established performance evidence.
qs: what we were seeing particularly with things like coding suggestions
There was no way that humanly possible they could go through and use some of the standard techniques.
how can I integrate this into my overall first pass review
they can just drop that production right into coding suggestions

kp.k: Predictive coding may persist as manual review declines
kp.d: Julie predicts manual document review will disappear but does not expect predictive coding to disappear. She reports that some users employ generative coding suggestions to create seed sets, then apply traditional predictive coding to a million or two million documents because it is free in Everlaw. This is a hybrid workflow and cost rationale, not evidence that manual review has already ended.
qs: predictive coding is still a really good tool and it's free in Everlaw.

a lot of folks that are using the coding suggestions are doing that to create their seed set and then they're using traditional predictive coding when you're going against you know a million or two million documents cuz it's free.
I don't think predictive coding is going away. I think manual document review is going away.

kp.k: Discovery redesign includes speculative prompt exchange
kp.d: Julie hopes AI could reduce discovery costs through an initial production of the most responsive documents followed by additional requests. She also relays a suggestion from another conference session that parties might exchange questions for Deep Dive instead of conventional production requests. She presents this as a desired future possibility, potentially beyond her retirement in three years, not an existing procedure or legal reform.
qs: maybe round one of discovery is we produce the most responsive and then you can come back and ask for more.
the other side their requests for production are the questions they want us to ask deep dive and that's what they get and and we do the same thing.
it probably won't be before I retire in three years

kp.d: Julie reports using extraction features in corporate contract and lease reviews to compile information from thousands of documents into tables, replacing an activity performed by paralegals and lawyers. She expects a suite of tools to touch every part of e-discovery. Joshua describes Everlaw's product strategy as embedding relevant capabilities across investigation and litigation through final trial preparation rather than supplying an isolated chatbot.
qs: we're using that even in the corporate world for contract review and lease reviews
you can go across again thousands and thousands of documents and have it extract pieces of information into a table.
if you think about parallegals and lawyers taking information and putting it into a table so they can use it, it does all that for you now.
it's not just a chatbot that exists in this sort of moment in time in the overall investigation or litigation life cycle.

kp.k: Document grounding does not eliminate verification requirements
kp.d: Julie argues that working against the firm's own documents and testing on familiar cases builds confidence, while still requiring validation. After the host raises hallucinations, Joshua explicitly rejects any promise of eliminating them completely. He emphasizes restricting attention to relevant documents and making cited text accessible so legal professionals can check reasoning against sources. Familiar-case confidence is experiential testing, not a reported hallucination-rate benchmark.
qs: it's still important to validate
he knew the case he knew what the answer should be.
any provider who says we can eliminate hallucinations 100% is not telling the truth.
Here is the actual document that it's pointing to and here is the text in that document.

kp.k: AI pricing differentiates small tasks from bulk processing
kp.d: Joshua attributes substantial generative AI costs to using leading models and processing large corpora. He announces inclusion of single-document summaries, individual coding suggestions and writing-assistant functions in the existing core per-gigabyte rate without increasing that rate. Large batch actions remain separately charged, with an announced 40% price reduction. These are vendor pricing statements, not evidence of equivalent reductions in clients' total legal bills.
qs: if you're looking at 10 million documents um that cost is quite substantial.
we're going to be including in the core per gigabyte rate and we're not raising that rate.
for these large batch actions um where you're potentially going to be do coding suggestions on a large corpus, uh we are still going to be charging for those.
we are reducing the price on that by 40%.

kp.k: Firm investment combines leadership commitment and selective purchasing
kp.d: Julie credits managing-partner support for the firm's willingness to invest. She describes evaluating fit rather than buying every product, benefiting from early-adopter pricing, and evaluating approximately 15 agentic platforms before choosing a UK startup. She considers many individual Everlaw tasks inexpensive but acknowledges that processing 10 million documents creates material costs.
qs: managing partner came out and we are doing genai.
you can't buy every tool on the market.
we evaluated and did demos on I think 15 different platforms
we ended up settling on one that we're pretty happy with which was a startup company out of the UK

kp.k: Lawyer roles may emphasize judgment under efficiency pressure
kp.d: Adam expects reasoning, independent judgment, strategy and interpersonal work to remain important even if manual review becomes unnecessary. He notes that he still reviews documents and that lawyers must conduct depositions, prepare motions, check case law and manage clients. He expresses uncertainty and some concern about job consequences rather than predicting universal replacement, while warning that clients may demand AI-enabled efficiency even where firms do not.
qs: there's still going to be reasoning, independent judgment, strategy decisions, and other soft things that I think are going to come to the forefront.
I I'm certainly still reviewing my documents.
I don't think it will replace everyone completely.
it might not be your firm that demands it. It might be your clients.

kp.k: Begin experimentation without exposing confidential information
kp.d: Julie recommends hands-on experimentation even without a purchased private tool, provided public tools receive no private or client information. She reports building a secure internal chat within roughly six months of ChatGPT's release. Joshua likewise urges organizations to establish policies and obtain or activate tools. Julie cautions, through personal observations, against assuming younger people automatically know or use AI; training remains necessary.
qs: you can still use the public tools as long as you're not putting private or client client information or private information.
we actually built our own secure chat early on, probably within 6 months of of chat GPT coming out.
if you don't have the policy in place well try to get that policy in place
I don't even know that the younger generation is definitely on board with it yet

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The panel describes AI as accelerating litigation insight and automating document tasks, while predicting less manual review, greater emphasis on strategy, and pressure to adopt. Broader efficiency and discovery-system changes remain prospective.
pts.d: Adam Borgman argues that firms must first understand their existing workflows to identify where AI can genuinely create efficiency. Julie Brown describes combining firm-wide process mapping with immediate experimentation and agent building. Brown reports that AI already surfaces insights and produces document-review savings, but says broader time savings have not yet materialised because training, prompting and experimentation require investment. Borgman's deposition-summary example illustrates rapid identification of a linguistic connection, leaving the lawyer to decide its strategic significance. Joshua Schnol describes Deep Dive as enabling natural-language questioning across entire document collections, with links and relevance information that support human verification. Brown identifies present applications in investigations, quality control after predictive coding, and deposition preparation. Borgman predicts that identifying both favourable and harmful evidence could shift litigation competition toward strategy and presentation; he says firms without comparable capabilities may be disadvantaged. Schnol describes customers moving from emergency use of coding suggestions toward systematic first-pass review. Brown predicts that manual document review will disappear but predictive coding will remain useful, particularly because it is included without additional charge in Everlaw. She also reports that extraction tools already automate tabulation for contract and lease review. Brown envisages discovery becoming more selective or eventually involving exchanged prompts, but presents this as a desired future rather than an established development. Schnol says grounding and source links support verification but do not eliminate hallucinations. Borgman expects continuing demand for human judgment, depositions, motion preparation, legal checking and client care, while predicting that firms or clients will demand AI-enabled efficiency. On costs, Schnol announces broader inclusion of smaller AI tasks in the existing platform rate and a 40% reduction in pricing for chargeable large-batch actions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of practitioner experiments, reported implementation experience, vendor beta and customer accounts, and announced pricing—not comparative benchmarks or measured productivity studies.
pts.d: Borgman's principal example is a sandbox test using a recently resolved case he knew thoroughly. The deposition-summary tool connected an initial medication question with later testimony about Tums. Borgman explicitly says he would not use that connection to impeach the witness; he treats it as a proof of concept for language-sensitive issue spotting, not demonstrated litigation success. This example concerns deposition summary, not Deep Dive. Brown reports testing Deep Dive on 300,000 documents and using it for investigations, deposition preparation and checks for material missed by searches or predictive coding. Schnol says the largest beta matter contained 10 million documents; this establishes a reported deployment scale, not a measured completeness or accuracy rate. Brown's statements about document-review savings and answer consistency are experiential and unquantified. Schnol's account of adoption moving from deadline-driven experiments to systematic review relies on customer observations, including a customer's last-minute-production example, rather than a disclosed study. The firm-wide adoption account includes a roughly ten-person process-mapping team, workshops, policies, training and tool evaluation. The 40% pricing reduction is a vendor announcement, not evidence of total client cost savings. Predictions about the disappearance of manual review, strategy-centred competition and prompt-based discovery have no quantified supporting forecasts in the transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current benefits are qualified by an experimental adoption stage, verification requirements and implementation costs; broader savings are anticipated within roughly six months, while structural discovery changes have no firm timetable.
pts.d: At the panel, Brown distinguishes existing document-review savings from broader drafting and task efficiencies that she expects probably within six months, as users improve their prompting and familiarity. The firm describes a roughly two-year adoption project, early policies after ChatGPT's November 2022 debut, workshops around July or August 2023, and purchases of suitable tools around January 2024; Brown qualifies some dates with uncertainty. Deep Dive is described as newly generally released following beta testing. Schnol describes a roughly six-month progression from emergency coding-suggestion experiments toward consideration of systematic first-pass review. Borgman's competitive-advantage claim is conditional on proving accuracy and making discovery decisions defensible, including explaining provenance, authenticity and process. His strategy-centred vision is explicitly theoretical and not yet playing out; he suggests the distinction changes once both sides possess such tools. Brown's prediction that manual review will disappear has no fixed deadline, while she does not expect her hoped-for discovery redesign before retirement in three years. Borgman notes that he still reviews documents. Brown's confidence in document-grounded tools is accompanied by a requirement to validate, and Schnol expressly rejects complete elimination of hallucinations. Pricing changes apply differently to smaller included tasks and chargeable large-batch actions. Brown recommends experimentation with public tools only without private or client information.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern litigation teams, document reviewers, practice-technology staff and corporate clients, with additional implications for contract-review roles and public-sector adoption.
pts.d: Litigators, especially those handling large document collections, are described as gaining faster access to evidence and more time for substantive follow-up and strategy. Borgman applies this specifically to employers and companies defending employment claims, which could investigate their opponents' strongest evidence earlier. Opposing counsel may lose the tactical benefit of last-minute productions when recipients already have appropriate coding protocols. Manual reviewers face the most explicit task-substitution prediction. Lawyers and paralegals performing extraction and tabulation in contract and lease reviews are already described as having that work automated. Borgman does not predict complete replacement of lawyers: he emphasises ongoing responsibility for judgment, verification, advocacy and client relationships. Clients may demand efficiency even where firms do not. Practice-technology and information-management teams take on process mapping, agent building, training and implementation work. Schnol reports uneven adoption among organisations and suggests public-sector policy constraints may be more complicated. Brown cautions against assuming younger people will automatically drive adoption and reports that generative AI has personally encouraged her to remain in work longer. The discussion does not provide a quantified employment forecast, establish client-wide net savings, or make an access-to-justice claim.
